title: The city he built
hook: a pool, a bazaar and a sangat: tradition says Guru Ram Das built a place for ordinary life to be holy

segments.voice: Yesterday, longing for sight: the ache of separation in Guru Ram Das's hymn, and darsan, the seeing that heals it. Your line was longing for sight. Who did you miss, and did it send you anywhere? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-seven.

Step out of the gate of the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, and you're not in a quiet garden. You're in the street. Shops, carts, the smell of frying, someone selling bangles, someone haggling over cloth. The Guru's house and a busy market sit right next to each other, and the crowd doesn't seem to find that strange. Sikh tradition says it was planned that way, from the start, by the Guru who began the city. Today, the end of the week, and the city he built.
screen: `OUT OF THE GATE, INTO THE STREET.` → `HOLY PLACE, BUSY MARKET.` → `PLANNED THAT WAY, TRADITION SAYS.`

segments.voice: Earlier on this path we heard about the pool itself, the pool of nectar at Amritsar. Today, look at what grew around it. Tradition says Guru Ram Das didn't only dig a pool. He invited traders and craftspeople to come and settle, to open shops, to build a bazaar beside it. So the town tradition calls Ramdaspur, after him, had three things in one place: a pool to wash in, a market to work in, and a sangat to sing with. That's an idea, not just a town plan. Look back over this week. The Gursikh's morning: rise, bathe, remember. After the morning: work, sitting and standing, with the Name. Blessing others: help someone else remember. The city is that same salok, built in brick. The bath is the pool. The work is the bazaar. The others are the sangat. In this picture, holiness isn't kept in a separate place you visit now and then. It's laid out next to the shop. His son, Guru Arjan, later praised the town in a salok, paraphrased: I have seen every place, and none is like you. The Creator himself founded you. Ramdaspur is thick with people, beyond compare. Notice what he praises. Not empty silence. A crowded town. A place full of people buying and selling, where the Name is sung in the middle of it all. That's what holy in the market means. Not that the market is perfect. That the market is not outside the reach of the Name.
screen: `A POOL, A BAZAAR, A SANGAT.` · `THE WEEK'S SALOK, BUILT IN BRICK.` · `NONE IS LIKE YOU, RAMDASPUR.` · `THE MARKET IS NOT OUTSIDE IT.` · then, large: `THE CITY HE BUILT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk through a market mindfully, today or the next time you shop. For now, in the sit, rehearse it. Picture the store or the street you'll be in. The lights, the noise, the line at the counter. Picture yourself walking through it a little slower than usual, feeling your feet, noticing the faces of the people working there. Let one breath, at the counter, be a remembering. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on that breath. The bell holds the time.
The city he built. Tradition says Guru Ram Das gathered a pool, a bazaar and a sangat in one town, Ramdaspur, now Amritsar. Today's word.
Your line: holy in the market. The next time you pay for something today, look up at the person across the counter and thank them properly. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Pilgrims to the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar walk through the old bazaars around it on their way in and out, and Sikhs remember Guru Ram Das as the Guru who began the city.

fork.setup: you're beginning a town around a sacred pool. tradition says Guru Ram Das did what?
options: kept it quiet, with no shops nearby.
invited traders and craftspeople to settle beside it.
allowed only pilgrims to live there.
fork.reveal: tradition says he invited traders and craftspeople, so the pool, the bazaar and the sangat grew up together.

original.note: Ramdaspur, the town of Ram Das: the name Guru Arjan uses for the city in his salok.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy places are kept apart from shops and noise.
what it means: a pool, a bazaar and a sangat in one town: ordinary life within reach of the Name.
what a scholar hears: 'vasdi saghan apaar anoop ramdas pur', Guru Arjan's praise of the crowded town.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Mahala 5, Ang 1362 (I have seen every place, none is like you; the Creator founded you; Ramdaspur is thick with people, beyond compare)

notes: The salok 'dithe sabhe thaav nahi tudh jehiaa... vasdi saghan apaar anoop ramdas pur' is attributed to Guru Arjan at Ang 1362, from memory; please confirm Ang, author and paraphrase.
Guru Ram Das inviting traders and craftspeople to settle and build a bazaar is given as tradition; no numbers of trades are given. Please confirm.
The hook avoids superlatives about the Harmandir Sahib; its description of the street outside the gate is general and should be checked against the present-day surroundings.
This is a week end (days 1191–1197); the teach looks back over the Gursikh salok days. The pool itself was taught on day 55.
